source: He-Yueya, Goodman, Brunskill (2024) Evaluating and Optimizing Educational Content with Language Model Judgments
finding: GPT-3.5 acting as an expert judge of simulated learners reproduced the expertise reversal effect. Low-expertise personas gained from worked examples over practice. High-expertise personas showed no difference.
numbers: 120 student personas, math word problems (systems of equations), gpt-3.5-turbo-16k at temperature 0. 8 instruction problems; worked solutions for problems 1,3,5,7. Low-expertise: worked > practice (significant). High-expertise: no significant difference. No exact p in the text I read.
quote: LM-based SEEs can accurately replicate the Expertise Reversal Effect
limits: The model has likely seen the original studies in training. The result is a null (no difference), not a true reversal where examples hurt. Simulated, not humans.
agent_relevance: A model can predict whether a lesson helps a given class, but it needs a code check against real pass rates.

source: He-Yueya, Goodman, Brunskill (2024) Evaluating and Optimizing Educational Content with Language Model Judgments (variability effect)
finding: Same pipeline also reproduced the variability effect: varied examples help when load is low (worked examples) and not when load is high (practice only).
numbers: 120 personas split into 4 groups (low/high variability x practice/worked), 6 post-test problems, gpt-3.5-turbo-16k.
limits: Same contamination and simulation caveats.
agent_relevance: Lesson value depends on current load of the solver: the same lesson can be good or neutral depending on state.

source: He-Yueya, Goodman, Brunskill (2024) Evaluating and Optimizing Educational Content with Language Model Judgments (why not direct simulation)
finding: The authors first tried to make the model play the student. It could not keep a stable knowledge level before and after instruction, so they switched to model-as-expert-evaluator.
numbers: Qualitative; paper Appendix A. No numbers read.
limits: No numbers for this point.
agent_relevance: Asking a model to act weaker than it is does not work reliably. Vary what the agent is shown, not who it pretends to be.

source: Song et al. (2026) Knowledge-level simulation of novice AI students by machine unlearning
finding: Prompting an LLM to act like a novice does not keep it at novice level. It slips into expert-level explanations. Unlearning gave more novice-like answers than prompt-only baselines, and the agent relearned part of the removed knowledge from teaching dialogue.
numbers: Python-concept multiple-choice dataset; abstract reports direction only (more novice-like than prompts; measurable partial recovery). Exact percentages not extracted.
quote: even when prompted to act like a novice, the LLMs can still produce expert-level explanations
limits: Small domain; abstract-level results only in my read.
agent_relevance: A persona prompt is not a competence estimate. Per-class competence must come from measured pass rates.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) When Correct Demonstrations Hurt: Rethinking the Role of Exemplars in In-Context Learning
finding: Demonstrations that are correct but drawn from a shifted input style can lower accuracy, sometimes below zero-shot. Harm grows with the share of perturbed exemplars and falls with model size.
numbers: SST-2, accuracy mean over 100 runs. Llama-2-7B-Chat: zero-shot 96.4; 0% perturbed 100.0; 50% 95.0; 75% 80.3; 100% 56.9. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: zero-shot 98.2; 100% perturbed 66.0. Gemma-4 2B: zero-shot 100.0; 100% perturbed 83.2.
limits: Harm appears mostly in small models. Task is near ceiling zero-shot, so clean demos add almost nothing there.
agent_relevance: A correct lesson can still hurt. Test each lesson against the no-lesson arm; show lessons only where failures are measured.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) When Correct Demonstrations Hurt: Rethinking the Role of Exemplars in In-Context Learning (large models)
finding: Larger models were robust to the shifted demonstrations. The paper says degradation is stronger for smaller models, harder tasks and higher perturbation ratios. This is not a size-grows-harm pattern.
limits: Harm here comes from distribution shift of the lesson, not from redundancy. Do not equate it with expertise reversal.
agent_relevance: Two separate failure mechanisms for lessons: redundancy (strong solver) and mismatch (weak solver). Log both.

source: Honda, Murakami, Zhang (2025) Distilling Many-Shot In-Context Learning into a Cheat Sheet
finding: On academic reasoning benchmarks, adding many demonstrations did not help and on MATH500 hurt. A short distilled cheat sheet beat both.
numbers: gemini-1.5-pro-002, accuracy averaged over 3 runs. MATH500: 8-shot 86.3, 400-shot 82.3, cheat sheet 88.0. GSM8K: 8-shot 94.5, 400-shot 95.1, cheat sheet 94.5. GPQA: 8-shot 57.1, 250-shot 56.7, cheat sheet 60.4.
limits: Appendix result. Differences on GSM8K and GPQA are within noise for 3 runs.
agent_relevance: More lessons per prompt is not better. A compact distilled lesson can beat a long library.

source: Honda, Murakami, Zhang (2025) Distilling Many-Shot In-Context Learning into a Cheat Sheet (GPT-4.1)
finding: With GPT-4.1 on MATH500, GSM8K and GPQA there was no gain from few-shot to many-shot. The authors explain that the knowledge is already encoded, so a few demos are enough.
numbers: Figure 4 in the paper (values not in the text I read); scores averaged over three runs.
quote: the academic knowledge assessed by these benchmarks is sufficiently general and already robustly encoded
limits: Interpretation is the authors' guess, not a controlled expertise manipulation.
agent_relevance: If the base model already solves a class, extra worked examples for it add cost and no gain. Ablate before keeping.

source: Zou, Khalifa, Wang (2024) On Many-Shot In-Context Learning for Long-Context Evaluation
finding: Which tasks gain from more demonstrations depends on task type. Classification and summarization improved. Translation and reasoning showed no clear trend.
numbers: Models include Llama-3.1, Gemini-1.5-Pro, Qwen2-72B, GLM-4, Mistral. On similar-sample tasks performance rose to about 32k tokens and then fell for most open models; Mistral-Large (123B) dropped dramatically beyond 32k, worse than Phi-3-Mini.
limits: Long-context failure is mixed with demonstration redundancy.
agent_relevance: For reasoning classes, adding examples is not a reliable lever. Decide per class.

source: Zou, Khalifa, Wang (2024) On Many-Shot In-Context Learning for Long-Context Evaluation (difficulty)
finding: Harder tasks degraded at shorter contexts than easier tasks, so the example budget that works depends on task difficulty.
numbers: Llama-3.1-70B lost accuracy on level-4 and level-5 symbolic tasks before level-1.
limits: Mixed with length effects.
agent_relevance: Budget examples by class difficulty, not with one global number.

source: Wei et al. (2023) Larger language models do in-context learning differently
finding: Small models mostly follow priors and ignore contradicting in-context labels. Large models can override priors and learn the mapping from the examples. Instruction tuning strengthens reliance on priors more than input-label learning.
numbers: Flipped-label and semantically-unrelated-label ICL across GPT-3, InstructGPT, Codex, PaLM, Flan-PaLM; ability emerges with scale. Exact accuracies not extracted.
limits: Classification; older models.
agent_relevance: What the model already holds decides how much the examples matter. Per-class measured accuracy is our proxy for prior knowledge.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1
finding: The authors report that few-shot prompting consistently degrades R1 and advise zero-shot. A case where examples hurt a model that already reasons well.
numbers: Statement only. No table of numbers in the section I read.
quote: Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.
limits: Authors' observation, no controlled experiment shown. An outside toy blog test is not authoritative.
agent_relevance: For a strong reasoning solver, default to no worked example. Add one only on a class where the plain arm fails.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
finding: Step-by-step prompting raised average accuracy on non-reasoning models, but made several models worse on questions they would otherwise always get right.
numbers: GPQA Diamond, 198 questions, 25 trials each (N=4950). Average rating CoT vs direct: Gemini Flash 2.0 +0.135 (p<.001), Sonnet 3.5 +0.117 (p<.001), GPT-4o-mini +0.044 (p=.067). 100%-correct metric: Sonnet 3.5 +0.101; GPT-4o +0.01 (ns); Gemini Flash 2.0 -0.131; Gemini Pro 1.5 -0.172. CoT took 35-600% (5-15 s) longer.
limits: One benchmark, simple CoT prompt, temperature 0.
agent_relevance: Item-level reversal: the scaffold helps weak items and hurts mastered ones. Supports gating a scaffold by measured class competence.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting (reasoning models)
finding: For reasoning models (o3-mini, o4-mini, Gemini Flash 2.5) explicit CoT gave marginal accuracy gains at best while adding time and tokens. Many non-reasoning models already do CoT by default, so the prompt changes little.
numbers: Same GPQA Diamond design. Exact differences for reasoning models not extracted here.
limits: Only three reasoning models.
agent_relevance: A scaffold the model already runs internally is redundant. Do not stack a thinking scaffold on a thinking model.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: A meta-analysis of 110 papers (1,218 comparisons) plus their own tests on 20 datasets and 14 models: CoT gain is large only on math and symbolic tasks and near zero elsewhere.
numbers: Mean CoT gain: symbolic +14.2, math +12.3, logical +6.9. Top three categories: 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. Other categories: 56.8 vs 56.1.
limits: Compute is not matched between CoT and direct, which the authors flag.
agent_relevance: Scaffold value is class-dependent. Apply only to classes where the gain is shown.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think
finding: A reasoning model trained to choose thinking or no-thinking by difficulty cut length and kept or improved accuracy. It used no-thinking mostly on easy problems and thinking on hard ones.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, lambda=0.05: GSM8K 83.1 vs 79.0 thinking; MATH500 82.0 vs 80.6; AIME24 31.0 vs 29.4; average +2.4 points and -53.0% length. NoThinking ratio: GSM8K 86.9%, MATH500 76.8%, AIME24 40.4%. 7B: -40.1% length, +2.3 points (abstract-level).
quote: Thinking only brings notable benefits for challenging problems
limits: Needs RL training. For the 1.5B model forced NoThinking alone was worse (GSM8K 69.8, MATH500 67.2, AIME24 14.0).
agent_relevance: Machine fading: scaffolding withdrawn as competence grows, chosen per item. Our code gate on class pass rate is the training-free analogue.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think (difficulty levels)
finding: On MATH500 the 7B model picked NoThinking on most Level-1 problems and Thinking progressively more as level rose.
numbers: Figure 3 (values garbled in text extraction; Level-1 NoThinking share high, Level-5 low).
limits: Figures not tabulated in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Supports a per-class gate where easy classes get no scaffold.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks
finding: Hand-curated skills (procedural lessons) raised agent pass rates on average, but the gain varied by model and domain. This is the closest agent-loop test of lesson libraries.
numbers: 87 tasks, 8 domains, 18 model-harness configurations, matched no-skills vs curated. Average pass 33.9% to 50.5% (+16.6 pp; normalized gain 25.5%). Per-configuration gain +4.1 to +25.7 pp. Weakest: OpenHands + Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite +4.1 pp.
limits: Skills add context, so length is confounded (authors say length-matched controls are future work).
agent_relevance: Lesson libraries pay off unevenly. Matches S0: show lessons only where they help.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks (self-generated)
finding: Skills written by the model itself were worse than no skills.
numbers: Pass rate no-skills / self-generated / curated: Claude Code + Opus 4.7 43.0 / 34.9 / 61.2; Codex + GPT-5.5 46.8 / 35.5 / 66.5 (gap -11.3); Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro 36.0 / 24.5 / 60.8 (gap -11.5). Self-generated minus none: -8.1, -11.3, -11.5 pp.
limits: Deficit mixes content quality, skill discovery failure and creator-solver interference. Table columns were garbled in extraction; Codex row inferred from the stated gaps.
agent_relevance: The agent must not write its own lessons and then trust them without a held-out code test (G3).

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks (domain and priors)
finding: Skills help most where pretraining is thin and least where it is strong. A domain-level expertise-reversal pattern.
numbers: Math and OR gain +9.7 pp (among the least). Top ten tasks mean +67.0 pp, e.g. prefix-cache replay 1.9% to 94.4%.
quote: domains with stronger pretraining and tooling coverage benefit less
limits: Domain labels are coarse; not a within-learner design.
agent_relevance: Order lessons by measured weakness. Strong classes get none.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks (harm and size)
finding: Skills hurt on some tasks, and compact skills beat exhaustive ones. A skill can displace a better default strategy.
numbers: 13 of 87 tasks had negative deltas (largest -7.4 pp). Skill length: compact +19.0, standard +21.5, detailed +14.5, comprehensive +0.7 pp. MiniMax M2.7 with skills 34.9% beat stronger no-skill baselines 32.7% and 29.7%.
limits: Task counts per cell are small.
agent_relevance: Keep lessons short. A lesson that displaces a stronger default is the agent form of expertise reversal.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks (strongest not biggest gainers)
finding: The strongest systems were not the biggest gainers. Largest lifts came from mid-ranked configurations.
numbers: With skills: OpenHands + GPT-5.5 67.3%, Codex + GPT-5.5 66.5%, Claude Code + Opus 4.7 61.2%. Largest lifts: OpenHands + GLM 5.1 +25.7 pp, Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro +24.8, OpenHands + DeepSeek V4 Pro +23.2.
limits: Lift also depends on baseline headroom.
agent_relevance: Compare lift to the model's own baseline per class, not to a global average.

source: Sankaranarayanan (2026) Mitigating Epistemic Debt in Generative AI-Scaffolded Novice Programming using Metacognitive Scripts
finding: Unrestricted AI help made novices as productive as scaffolded help but left them unable to maintain code without it. A teach-back explanation gate cut the failure rate.
numbers: N=78 between subjects. Both AI groups beat manual on functional utility (p<.001), not different from each other (p=.64). 30-minute AI-blackout maintenance task: 77% failure for unrestricted AI vs 39% scaffolded. Gate cut epistemic debt by 41.7 points (69.3 to 27.6) at 14.2 minutes cost. Built on Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
limits: Online-recruited participants; one task; immediate test only.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that never fades creates dependence. For an agent, test with lessons removed.

source: Sankaranarayanan (2026) Mitigating Epistemic Debt in Generative AI-Scaffolded Novice Programming using Metacognitive Scripts (fading proposed)
finding: The paper names expertise reversal as the basis for adaptive friction that fades as competence grows, but states it only as future work.
numbers: No data on fading in this paper.
limits: Not tested.
agent_relevance: Fading in LLM tutoring is still mostly a proposal; few measured tests exist.

source: Hou et al. (2026) Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
finding: A tutor that raises support after failure and fades it after take-up kept the learner's decision work close to a question-only tutor, while giving more concrete help and causing less frustration. The tutor used Claude Haiku.
numbers: Within-subjects, 131 adult learners, 3 Python tasks, 3 tutors (contingent CoMeT, unrestricted assistant, question-only). Fading logged on 551 occasions, 515 coded, scored on whether fading held. Full answer surrendered in 1 session in 16 vs 1 in 6 for the question-only tutor.
limits: Adult lab sample; abstract text garbled in extraction so some comparisons are read approximately. No delayed test.
agent_relevance: The ladder rule is code: climb on failure, drop on take-up. This is Salden-style adaptive fading and fits S0.

source: Anand and Idan (2026) Generative AI and the Productivity Divide
finding: In a randomized self-study experiment, LLM access raised average performance, but prior knowledge did not predict who benefited. Skill at using the AI did.
numbers: Treatment x pre-exam interaction p=0.2; Treatment x GPA p=0.59; three-way interaction with AI interaction competence p<0.05. In the no-LLM arm gains fell with prior knowledge; in the LLM arm that slope flattened.
limits: Working paper; sample size not extracted; no explicit expertise-reversal crossover shown.
agent_relevance: A null for the classic prediction: baseline score alone did not predict benefit. Use measured use-of-help signals as well.

source: Scaffolding collapse in Socratic tutors, Scaffold-Preserving Representation Alignment (SPRA)
finding: LLM Socratic tutors drift into giving the answer under sustained student pressure. The failure is over-help, not too little help.
numbers: Qwen3-8B: abstract reports collapse rate 32%; table shows full method 36.0% (GPT-5.1 judge, 500 test problems, 5 STEM areas) vs SFT only 47.0% and online-updated reference 63.5%. Judge choice moves the rate: Claude-Haiku-4.5 judge 84.5%, human 35.2%.
limits: Red-teaming setup, not real students. Abstract (32) and table (36) differ. Authors not extracted.
agent_relevance: If a model gives hints, code must cap the help level; the model drifts toward full answers.

source: Salden, Aleven, Schwonke, Renkl (2010) The expertise reversal effect and worked examples in tutored problem solving
finding: Older AI system: a Cognitive Tutor with worked examples faded adaptively to each student beat the same tutor with fixed fading and plain problem solving, in one lab and one classroom experiment.
numbers: Search snippets only: adaptive > fixed fading > problem solving; the 2008 version reports the edge on delayed transfer. No effect sizes read.
limits: Not opened. Numbers unverified.
agent_relevance: The rule-based fading controller. Our class-pass-rate gate is the same idea with a different signal.

source: Gonzaga, Vassar, Jiang (2026) CS TA perceptions on LLM-generated faded worked examples (SIGCSE TS)
finding: Search summary: a randomized trial found LLM-generated faded worked examples gave no significant advantage over standard feedback training in cognitive load.
numbers: Per search summary N=27 teaching assistants; nothing else. Already in 01_worked_example_research as c17.
limits: Not opened this session; small N; null result.
agent_relevance: An honest null for LLM-made fading in humans.
